{{Short description|Cryptographic solution}}
"'''The Magic Words are Squeamish Ossifrage'''" was the solution to a challenge [[ciphertext]] posed by the inventors of the [[RSA (algorithm)|RSA]] [[cipher]] in 1977. The problem appeared in [[Martin Gardner]]'s ''[[Mathematical Games column]]'' in the August 1977 issue of ''[[Scientific American]]''.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Singh|first1=Simon|title=The Code Book: The Science of Secrecy From Ancient Egypt To Quantum Cryptography|date=1999|publisher=Anchor Books|location=New York|isbn=978-0-385-49532-5|pages=[https://archive.org/details/codebook00simo/page/278 278]|edition=First Anchor Books|url-access=registration|url=https://archive.org/details/codebook00simo/page/278}}</ref> It was solved in 1993–94 by a large, joint computer project co-ordinated by [[Derek Atkins]], [[Michael Graff]], [[Arjen Lenstra]] and [[Paul Leyland]].<ref>{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.wired.com/1996/03/crackers/|title=Wisecrackers|magazine=WIRED|language=en-US|access-date=2016-05-24|date=March 1996}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |author1=Atkins, D. |author2=Graff, M. |author3=Lenstra, A.K. |author4=Leyland, P.C. |title=Advances in Cryptology — ASIACRYPT'94 |chapter=The magic words are squeamish ossifrage |editor1-last=Pieprzyk |editor1-first=J. |editor2-last=Safavi-Naini |editor2-first=R. |date=1995 |pages=261–277 |doi=10.1007/BFb0000440 |chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/BFb0000440 |access-date=15 March 2025 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=917 |publisher=Springer |location=Berlin, Heidelberg|isbn=978-3-540-59339-3 |url=http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/149461 |chapter-url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name="Yan2012">{{cite book |last=Yan |first=Song Y. |title=Computational Number Theory and Modern Cryptography |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=eLAV586iF-8C&pg=RA1-PA106 |date=28 November 2012 |publisher=John Wiley & Sons |isbn=978-1-118-18861-3 |pages=1–}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|url=http://bit-player.org/wp-content/extras/bph-publications/AmSci-1994-07-Hayes-RSA-129.pdf |date=July 1994|last1=Hayes|first1=Brian|title=The magic words are squeamish ossifrage |journal=Scientific American |volume=82 |issue=4 |pages=312–316|bibcode=1994AmSci..82..312H }}</ref> More than 600 volunteers contributed [[Central processing unit|CPU]] time from about 1,600 machines (two of which were [[fax]] machines) over six months. The coordination was done via the [[Internet]] and was one of the first such projects.

''Ossifrage'' ('bone-breaker', from Latin) is an older name for the [[bearded vulture]], a scavenger famous for dropping animal bones and live tortoises on top of rocks to crack them open. The 1993–94 effort began the tradition of using the words "squeamish ossifrage" in [[cryptanalysis|cryptanalytic]] challenges.

The difficulty of [[RSA problem|breaking the RSA cipher]]—recovering a [[plaintext]] message given a ciphertext and the public key—is connected to the difficulty of [[integer factorization|factoring]] large numbers. While it is not known whether the two problems are mathematically equivalent, factoring is currently the only publicly known method of directly breaking RSA. The [[decryption]] of the 1977 ciphertext involved the factoring of a 129-digit (426 bit) number, [[RSA-129]], in order to recover the plaintext.

[[Ron Rivest]] estimated in 1977 that factoring a 125-digit semiprime would require 40 [[1000000000000000 (number)|quadrillion]] years, using the best [[algorithm]] known and the fastest computers of the day.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Gardner|first=Martin|title=Mathematical Games, August 1977|url=http://simson.net/ref/1977/Gardner_RSA.pdf|journal=Scientific American|volume=237|issue=2|pages=120–124|doi=10.1038/scientificamerican0877-120|year=1977}}</ref> In their original paper they recommended using 200-digit (663 bit) primes to provide a margin of safety against future developments,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Rivest|first1=R. L.|last2=Shamir|first2=A.|last3=Adleman|first3=L.|date=1978-02-01|title=A Method for Obtaining Digital Signatures and Public-key Cryptosystems|url=https://people.csail.mit.edu/rivest/Rsapaper.pdf|journal=Commun. ACM|volume=21|issue=2|pages=120–126|doi=10.1145/359340.359342|issn=0001-0782|citeseerx=10.1.1.607.2677|s2cid=2873616}}</ref> though it may have only delayed the solution as a 200-digit semiprime was factored in 2005.<ref name=announce>[[Thorsten Kleinjung]] (2005-05-09), [http://www.crypto-world.com/announcements/rsa200.txt We have factored RSA200 by GNFS] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080322125316/http://www.crypto-world.com/announcements/rsa200.txt |date=2008-03-22 }}. Retrieved on 2008-03-10.</ref><ref>RSA Laboratories, [https://www.emc.com/emc-plus/rsa-labs/historical/rsa-200-factored.htm RSA-200 is factored!]. Retrieved on 2008-03-10.</ref> However, efficient factoring algorithms had not been studied much at the time, and a lot of progress was made in the following decades. Atkins et al. used the [[quadratic sieve]] algorithm invented by [[Carl Pomerance]] in 1981. While the asymptotically faster [[General number field sieve|number field sieve]] had just been invented, it was not clear at the time that it would be better than the quadratic sieve for 129-digit numbers. The memory requirements of the newer algorithm were also a concern.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Stinson |first1=D. R. |title=RSA, Factoring, and Squeamish Ossifrage |url=http://cacr.uwaterloo.ca/~dstinson/papers/cs877s7.ps |publisher=University of Waterloo | year=1995|accessdate=28 September 2015}}, Supplementary Material to the 1995 edition of his ''Cryptography Theory and Practice'', see [http://cacr.uwaterloo.ca/~dstinson/CTAP.html web page].</ref>

There was a US$100 prize associated with the challenge, which the winners donated to the [[Free Software Foundation]].

In 2015, the same RSA-129 number was factored in about one day, with the CADO-NFS open source implementation of number field sieve, using a commercial cloud computing service for about $30.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://natmchugh.blogspot.com/2015/03/the-magic-words-are-squeamish-ossifrage.html|title=Nat McHugh: The Magic Words are Squeamish Ossifrage - factoring RSA-129 using CADO-NFS|last=Mchugh|first=Nathaniel|date=2015-03-26|website=Nat McHugh|access-date=2016-05-25}}</ref>
